stops.title: Britannia begins
stops.text: Captain John LeBreton, a naval officer back from the War of 1812, received land on Lac Deschênes and laid out a village he called Britannia, eight years before Bytown, the town that became Ottawa.

stops.title: The forge at the crossroads
stops.text: George Winthrop built a log blacksmith shop where the Richmond and March roads met, some 8 km from Bytown. It still stands on its own spot, one of the very few log buildings from the first settlement that do.

stops.title: The cottagers' boat club
stops.text: Britannia had become a summer cottage colony. The cottagers founded the Britannia Aquatic Club, which met in an old sawmill on the water and raced war canoes before it took up sailing: today's Britannia Yacht Club.

stops.title: St. Stephen's
stops.text: One of the two churches of the fashionable resort, and the only one still standing.

stops.title: Britannia-on-the-Bay
stops.text: On 24 May 1900 the Ottawa Electric Railway opened its new park at the end of the streetcar line. Riders crossed the railway on a high footbridge to the beach, pavilions and a long pier, built in fifteen weeks on the rubble of a failed power canal and lit at night by ten arc lights.

stops.title: 25,000 on a Sunday
stops.text: On fine Sundays in July and August the streetcars carried up to 25,000 people out to Britannia. The steamer G.B. Greene, the 'Queen of the River', took 250 passengers at a time up the river; her anchor lies at the beach.

stops.title: Queensway Terrace
stops.text: Robert Campeau's firm bought 114 acres of the Arkell farm on Pinecrest Road and built family houses on more than 300 lots, one of Ottawa's first large postwar neighbourhoods.

stops.title: The last streetcar
stops.text: On 1 May 1959 the last car ran out to Britannia, on what had become Ottawa's last streetcar line. Buses took over.

stops.title: The plant and Mud Lake
stops.text: The city built the Britannia Water Purification Plant on the point from 1958 to 1961. Its causeway cut off a shallow bay of the river, which became Mud Lake, now the best birding spot in Ottawa.

stops.title: The Queensway cuts through
stops.text: Highway 417 was built along the old railway line and split Queensway Terrace in two, North and South.

stops.title: The floods
stops.text: The spring floods of 2017 and again 2019 put the shore of Britannia under water and badly damaged the trails around Mud Lake; the NCC has since rebuilt them and replaced the footbridge.
